title: THE PAYCHECK YOU NEVER WANTED: Why “The Wages of Sin Is Death” Still Applies Today
paragraphs:
THE PAYCHECK YOU NEVER WANTED: Why “The Wages of Sin Is Death” Still Applies Today
We modernized our language for sin. We renamed it, normalized it, excused it, monetized it, laughed about it, and sometimes even celebrated it. But changing the name of the poison never changed what the poison does. And the most terrifying part of Romans 6:23 may not be the word “death.” It may be the word “wages.”
There are Bible verses people love putting on coffee mugs.
Romans 6:23 usually isn’t one of them.
Because it refuses to flatter us.

It does not tell us that everything inside us should be trusted. It does not say that every desire deserves expression. It does not tell us that sin becomes harmless when culture approves of it, when enough people practice it, when celebrities celebrate it, when algorithms promote it, or when we find a softer word to describe it.
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
That sentence was written nearly two thousand years ago.
It knows the man deleting his browser history before his wife walks into the room.
It knows the woman smiling in church while bitterness has been quietly consuming her for years.
It knows the teenager who learned how to perform Christianity before learning how to surrender to Christ.
It knows the pastor who can preach repentance while secretly needing to repent.
It knows the person posting Bible verses publicly while privately feeding an addiction.
The sinner who does not even call it sin anymore.
And it knows something we desperately need to remember:
Maybe not in the way you expected.
Τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος
Ta gar opsōnia tēs hamartias thanatos.
The word translated “wages” is ὀψώνια — opsōnia.
It refers to pay, compensation, wages—what is received for service rendered. The word had associations with a soldier’s pay or provisions.
Paul does not merely describe death as an unfortunate possibility surrounding sin.
He describes death as sin’s wage.
Something sin produces according to its terrible economy.
And then Paul does something breathtaking.
“The wages of sin is death, but the wages of righteousness are eternal life.”
Because if eternal life were something fallen human beings could earn, the Gospel would cease to be good news.
τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος
to de charisma tou theou zōē aiōnios
“but the gift of God [is] eternal life.”
And that difference is the heartbeat of Christianity.
You cannot put God into your debt.
You cannot accumulate enough religious points to purchase eternal life.
You cannot undo yesterday’s rebellion by behaving better tomorrow.
You cannot save yourself by becoming slightly more moral than the person sitting next to you.
And Paul refuses to leave that gift floating in vague spirituality.
He tells us exactly where it is found:
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν
en Christō Iēsou tō kyriō hēmōn
Not in comparing yourself with worse sinners.
That is why Romans 6:23 still applies today.
We simply became better at decorating it.
We call greed ambition when it benefits us.
We call lust harmless entertainment when nobody knows.
We call pride self-confidence even when it makes repentance almost impossible.
We call unforgiveness boundaries when what we really mean is that we secretly enjoy replaying another person's offense.
And sometimes we use legitimate psychological, cultural, or therapeutic language as camouflage for something Scripture is asking us to confront spiritually.
Not every painful emotion is evidence that someone has disobeyed God.
Jesus showed profound compassion toward suffering people.
But neither does compassion require us to pretend sin is harmless.
Christ did not come merely to make sinners feel more comfortable while remaining enslaved.
The angel's announcement concerning Jesus in Matthew 1:21 was astonishingly specific:
“He shall save his people from their sins.”
Because sin is deeper than bad habits.
And ultimately, apart from God's saving grace in Christ, sin ends in death.
Paul had already written in Romans 3:23:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
That word destroys our favorite escape route.
We love finding someone whose darkness looks darker than ours.
“At least I provide for my family.”
But heaven's courtroom does not operate on a curve.
The question is not whether you have sinned less spectacularly than somebody else.
The question is whether you have sinned.
Every one of us stands in desperate need of grace.
And this is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because the Gospel does not say good people go to heaven while bad people go to hell.
The Gospel announces something far more humbling:
Maybe this is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps there is something you have been negotiating with God about.
Something you keep renaming because calling it what Scripture calls it would require you to confront it.
Because the God who knows completely is also the God who calls sinners to repentance and offers mercy through His Son.
The cross was not merely an inspirational example of sacrificial love.
Scripture presents Christ's death as God's saving work for sinners.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we conquered every addiction.
Not after our thoughts became pure.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we finally became worthy.
“Fix yourself and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that the Son of God entered our ruin to accomplish what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
He went willingly to the cross.
The wages of sin is death...
and Christ walked directly into death.
First Peter 2:24 says that Christ “his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.”
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
This is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
So Christ pays what we cannot.
The lost cannot invent a road home.
“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
The cross declares that Christ's mercy is greater than the sinner who truly comes to Him.
But grace must never be confused with permission.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Grace is not God's permission slip for continuing comfortably in rebellion.
Grace breaks sin's claim over us.
Grace teaches us to say no.
Grace calls us out of hiding.
Grace does not merely pardon the rebel and then leave the rebel unchanged.
A Christian can find himself crying over the same temptation he thought he had defeated.
But there is an enormous difference between fighting sin and making peace with it.
Because perhaps you have been fighting something for months.
You fell again and thought, “Maybe God is finished with me.”
Do not use grace to excuse your sin.
But do not use your sin to deny the sufficiency of Christ either.
Cut off what continually feeds the temptation.
Pray when you don't feel spiritual.
If you fall, do not build a house where you fell.
Get up and return to Christ.
First John 1:9 gives struggling believers extraordinary hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe you've carried shame so long that it has started feeling like your identity.
And that is exactly where the Gospel reaches into the graveyard of identity.
The Bible does not sanitize their failures.
Scripture refuses to protect its heroes by editing away their scandals.
Because the glory belongs to God.
Grace does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace reveals that the scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Not by rewriting history as though sin never happened.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming people who could never redeem themselves.
The cross does not tell you your sin was insignificant.
The cross shows you just how serious sin is.
And then it shows you something else.
If sin were trivial, Calvary would make no sense.
If humans could save themselves, the cross would be unnecessary.
But if the wages of sin truly are death...
then suddenly the empty tomb becomes the greatest announcement the universe has ever heard.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have hope beyond the grave.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “be nicer.”
Jesus did not endure the cross merely to turn rude people into polite people.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
And perhaps the most dangerous person reading this article is not the person who knows he is broken.
Maybe it is the person convinced he isn't.
The person who has mastered religious appearances.
The person who can quote Scripture while resisting surrender.
The person who knows Christian vocabulary but has never truly come to Christ.
The person who knows how to lift hands in worship but refuses to release the secret idol in his heart.
You can know church culture without knowing Christ.
You can own five Bibles and still refuse the One they reveal.
You can sing about surrender while protecting the one room in your life where Jesus is not welcome.
You can have a Christian family.
Jesus did not say merely, “Admire Me.”
And following Jesus eventually leads us to places where something has to die.
The idol we keep asking God to bless rather than remove.
That is where Romans 6:23 stops being a verse on a page.
What is sin paying you right now?
Maybe it promised pleasure but pays shame.
Not every hardship in life is a direct payment for a particular personal sin; Scripture itself rejects such simplistic thinking.
But sin as a master still leads toward death.
That remains true whether the year is AD 60 or 2026.
But thank God Paul didn't put the period there.
There is another side of the sentence.
Sometimes the Gospel can hide inside a three-letter word.
“The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
The grave waits for every human body...
That does not mean everyone is automatically saved regardless of their response to Christ.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe.
Repentance is not purchasing salvation with remorse.
It is the turning of a heart toward God.
Faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
And perhaps that is exactly what needs to happen right now.
Not after you become more religious.
Confess the sin you've been defending.
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to give strangers the private details of your life.
Someone else reading the comments may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't merely think about them.
Send this privately if that would be wiser.
You never know which friend is smiling publicly while collapsing privately.
Because temptation has a strange ability to make us forget truths we were absolutely certain about yesterday.
Come back when sin starts advertising itself as freedom again.
Come back when shame tells you there is no road home.
Sin pays wages. God gives a gift. And that gift is found in Jesus Christ.

Supporting Christian ministry does not purchase God's favor, earn salvation, or make someone more righteous before Him. We glorify God by trusting and obeying Him, and Scripture teaches generosity as a willing response to grace rather than spiritual coercion.
But one practical way you can participate in spreading Gospel-centered resources is by helping support the work that produces and distributes them.
It is the gift of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That distinction matters because this entire article began with two words that belong to two completely different kingdoms:
The other reveals what God provides through Christ.
And eventually every one of us must decide which master we will serve.
Support faithful Gospel work when you are able.
Seek accountability where secrecy has become dangerous.
Come back to church if you've been hiding.
Come back to the feet of Jesus.
Do not walk away from Christ because you are ashamed of the very wounds you need Him to heal.
The Gospel was never written for people who successfully avoided having a scandal.
It was written for sinners who need grace.
And when the accuser points toward everything you have done and whispers, “Look at your record,” the Christian does not have to pretend the record is clean.
Because the final hope of the Christian is not:
Remember this when temptation whispers tonight:
Sin will always demand its wages—but Jesus still holds out the gift that death could never keep buried.
